title: Meridian Serif — Bulge-Bracket Client Cover
description: A centered, symmetrical cover slide engineered for institutional finance decks — a dark navy field anchors a bone-white transitional serif title, tracked small-caps subtitle, a client-name chip, and a hairline-gold ruled frame around the bottom wordmark. Where most corporate templates reach for boldness, this one reaches for gravitas.
philosophy: This design exists for boardrooms where visual excess reads as professional risk and restraint reads as competence. It refuses gradients, decorative iconography, and sans-serif convenience — choosing instead the authority of classical typesetting, precise optical spacing, and a single thin line of warm gold as the sole ornamental gesture. It is made for the managing director presenting a €2 billion mandate to a sovereign wealth fund, not for a growth-stage founder pitching seed capital. Space is the primary design element; everything else defers to it.
goodFor: Investment banking pitch book and client-deck cover pages
Private wealth and asset management quarterly review openers
M&A fairness opinion and deal-announcement title slides
Annual report and regulatory filing front-matter presentations
avoidFor: Startup pitch decks where founder personality and momentum must read on slide one
Consumer product launches requiring warmth, imagery, or brand color saturation
Chart-heavy operational reviews that demand dense information layouts
Internal team stand-ups or casual stakeholder check-ins
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like the cover page of a printed prospectus — institutional, unhurried, and architecturally precise. Mood is formal restraint: the weighted silence before a consequential announcement, not the forward momentum of a pitch. Compositional rhythm is fully centered and bilaterally symmetrical, with each text element suspended in its own vertical territory so that space itself becomes the dominant graphic element. Avoid diagonal tension, decorative layering, illustrative motifs, or any gesture that reads as warmth or informality — the single ruled line is the only ornament, and it must carry all ceremonial weight.

examples.layoutNotes: Centered 12-column grid with all typographic elements confined to columns 4–9, leaving the outer thirds as pure, untouched field. The client-name chip occupies its own line above the primary title, with the tracked small-caps subtitle sitting below it — each element separated by a deliberate vertical gutter that is never compressed. A full-width hairline rule in warm gold runs just above a bottom wordmark band, serving as the sole structural ornament. No header band, no page number, no edge bleed; the slide's authority derives entirely from axial symmetry and the generosity of its margins.

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like a page drawn from a printed institutional memorandum — composed, authoritative, and unhurried. Typographic hierarchy does all structural work: weight contrast and a single hairline rule delineate content zones without any iconography or decorative geometry. Rhythm is symmetrical with deliberate vertical breathing between elements so density never reads as urgency or disorder. Avoid illustrative embellishment of any kind; the authority of the slide must arise entirely from spatial discipline and the quiet precision of classical typesetting conventions.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with live content confined to columns 2–11, maintaining the template's characteristic outer breathing margin on both sides. A tracked small-caps section label anchors the top of the content zone, separated from the body by a full-width hairline rule spanning columns 2–11. Below the rule, substantive content — a structured two-column key-terms block, a centered stat callout, or a short attributed quotation — occupies columns 3–10 to preserve the symmetrical axis and avoid edge tension. Folio number and deck identifier sit in the bottom-right outer margin; no header band interrupts the dark field above the section label.
